parts.problem_md:
> **[case-study]**
> UDig is a large mining company based in country B. UDig is in the private sector. It supplies businesses in country B with 30% of the coal they need and the rest is imported. UDig now has eight mines but plans to close two of them. This will threaten 1800 employees with redundancy. The Managing Director said: ‘I blame the appreciation of country B’s exchange rate and new legal controls, including those to protect the environment. The Government should help private sector businesses.’

**Explain two **factors UDig should consider when deciding which mines to close.
parts.solution_md:
UDig should consider the level of output **[K]** when deciding which mines to close. The mines that extract the least amount of coal **[Ap]** could be closed, as they will generate less sales revenue for the business. For example, if two of the eight mines produce significantly less coal than the others, closing those would have the smallest impact on UDig's overall production and profits **[An]**

Another factor to consider is the number of employees at each mine **[K]**. Since 1800 jobs are threatened **[Ap]**, UDig could choose to close mines with fewer workers to save more jobs overall. For instance, if two mines employ only 500 workers combined, closing those would affect fewer employees than shutting down larger operations. This approach could help UDig minimise the negative impact on its workforce while still achieving necessary cost reductions **[An]**

>   - State a valid point relevant to the question → 1 K mark
>   - Apply it clearly to the business in the case study → 1 Ap mark
>   - Explain the impact using a cause–effect chain → 1 An mark
> 
> **Mark scheme**

>   - Level of output (1) where UDig extract the least amount of coal (1) could be closed as it will make less sales revenue. (1)
>   - Number of employees (1) as 1800 jobs threatened (1) if close sites with fewer employees the business may be able to save some of the jobs. (1)
>   - Ease of access (1) of the eight locations (1) as sites difficult to reach could help lower transport costs. (1)
>   - Pollution levels (1) as new legal controls have been introduced (1) so high polluting sites might be forced to close anyway. (1)

parts.problem_md: Do you think a service business should only employ part-time workers? **Justify **your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Part-time workers can help businesses with variable levels of demand **[K]**. Employing part-timers reduces labour costs when the business is not busy, as wages only need to be paid for hours worked. This allows for more flexible scheduling, making it easier to have enough staff during peak times** [An]**

However, full-time workers tend to be more committed to the business **[K]**, which could increase productivity and consistency of service, potentially improving the business's reputation and customer base **[An]**

A service business should not only employ part-time workers  **[E]**. A mix of full-time and part-time workers is possibly the best approach. This allows the business to benefit from the consistency and commitment of full-timers while still having the flexibility of part-timers to adjust staffing levels as needed **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - You are writing a mini-argument with a decision
> 
>   - Give one relevant reason to support your view → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this reason helps the business (cause-effect chain) →  1 An mark
>   - Give a different possible reason or viewpoint → 1 K mark
>   - Explain why this could also help the business → 1 An mark
>   - Make a decision — which argument is stronger or more important overall? → up to 2 E marks
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - Points might include:
> 
>   - Part-time:
>   
>     - When not working no need to pay wages [k] helping to reduce labour costs [an]
>     - Need to recruit/train more employees [k] taking more time/money [an]
>     - Could allow the business to recruit wider range of skills [k]
>     - More flexible hours/less likely to take time off for appointments [k]
>     - Easier to extend worker hours at busy times [k] or [an]
>     - Some employees may not be willing/want part-time jobs [k] so may miss out on possible candidates if not offered full-time option [an]
>   - Full-time:
>   
>     - Able to offer consistency of service [k] so could improve reputation/increase customers [an]
>     - Workers may be committed to business [k] which could increase the productivity of the business [an]
>     - Easier to communicate/update [k]
>     - Less workers needed [k]
>   - Other appropriate responses should also be credited
>   - Justification might include:
>   
>     - Part-time employees are only paid when they are working [k] reducing labour costs [an]. However, consistency of service may fall [k] which could damage the business reputation [an]. A service sector business especially should not have only part-time employees as service quality is vital for customer loyalty [eval] and therefore sales. [eval]
>   - The focus should be on the benefit/cost to the business not the worker
>   - Do not award points such as part-time workers are likely to be less tired, more motivated, lack skills, do not have a contract
>   - Do not award answers which confuse part-time with temporary/seasonal workers

> FBW manufactures watches using job production. It employs 5 full-time production employees. Each worker is offered regular training. Last year FBW sold 600 watches. The Managing Director plans to use break-even analysis to help decide whether to increase the price of its products. FBW’s current break-even chart is shown below.
> 
> ![Break-even chart showing fixed costs, total costs, and total revenue for FBW's watches across different production quantities, with cost and revenue in dollars.](assets/001-break-even-chart-showing-fixed-costs-total-costs.png)

**Explain two** benefits to FBW of having full-time employees.
parts.solution_md:
Firstly, full-time workers are likely to be more loyal to the company **[K]**. This means FBW's 5 production employees may stay with the business for longer, reducing the need to recruit and train new staff. As FBW uses job production **[Ap] **to make watches, having experienced workers who understand the specialised manufacturing process is crucial for maintaining quality **[An]**

Secondly, full-time employees are always available when needed **[K]**. This is important for FBW because they only sold 600 watches last year, which suggests they may have periods of lower demand **[Ap]**. Having full-time staff means they can quickly respond to changes in orders without needing to find temporary workers. This flexibility could be helpful when the Managing Director decides on price changes, as they can adjust production levels more easily **[An]**

parts.problem_md: Do you think it is better for a tertiary sector business to use full-time employees rather than part-time employees? **Justify **your answer.
parts.solution_md:
Full-time workers are often more familiar with the business **[K]**, which helps build customer relationships in stores or call centres, and improves the company's reputation. It's usually easier to communicate with full-time staff, leading to fewer errors and misunderstandings, which is likely to lead to more consistent customer service **[An]**

On the other hand, part-time employees allow businesses to extend their hours and cover busy periods flexibly **[K]**, minimising labour costs as the business only pays for hours these staff have actually worked **[An]**

Overall, I believe full-time employees are better for a tertiary sector business **[E] **because consistent service is crucial for customer loyalty. As quality of service is how customers often judge these businesses, having dedicated full-time staff is more likely to ensure repeat customers and maintain sales **[E]**

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

**SwiftLink Logistics**

SwiftLink Logistics is a private limited company that provides transportation and warehousing services in Country Y. Founded in 2005, SwiftLink has grown steadily and now employs 250 people across its five regional depots. The company specialises in delivering goods for online retailers and has benefitted from the recent growth in e-commerce.

SwiftLink's Managing Director, Alex Patel, is considering expanding the business by opening a new depot in the north of Country Y. This would require significant investment in vehicles, warehousing facilities, and staff. Alex believes this expansion could increase SwiftLink's annual revenue from \$15 million to \$20 million within two years.

However, SwiftLink faces several challenges. The logistics industry is becoming increasingly competitive, with new entrants using advanced technology to improve efficiency. SwiftLink's profit margin has decreased from 8% to 6% in the past year due to rising fuel costs and increased competition.

Alex is also concerned about employee motivation. A recent staff survey revealed that 40% of employees feel undervalued and overworked. The company currently uses a hierarchical management structure with five levels between the Managing Director and front-line staff.

To address these issues, Alex is considering implementing a flatter organisational structure and introducing a profit-sharing scheme for all employees. He believes these changes could improve motivation and productivity, but he's unsure how they might impact the business overall.

SwiftLink's Human Resources Director has suggested using internal recruitment to fill management positions in the new depot if the expansion goes ahead. However, some board members argue that external recruitment would bring in fresh ideas and expertise.

**Appendix 1: SwiftLink Logistics Financial Data**

| **Year** | **Revenue (\$m)** | **Profit margin       (%)** | **Labour turnover (%)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | 15 | 6 | 29 |
| 2021 | 13 | 8 | 22 |

Consider the advantages and disadvantages of the following two leadership styles Alex could adopt when implementing changes at SwiftLink Logistics.

- Democratic leadership style
- Autocratic leadership style

Which leadership style do you think would be most appropriate? **Justify **your answer.

Refer to the following [insert ](https://cdn.savemyexams.com/uploads/2024/10/swiftlink-logistics-case-study.pdf)when answering the question
parts.solution_md:
A democratic leadership style would involve Alex consulting employees before making decisions about expansion or restructuring **[Ap]**. This could generate ideas to reduce costs and improve efficiency, addressing SwiftLink's decreasing profit margin (from 8% to 6%) **[Ap]**. It could significantly improve motivation **[An]**, which is much-needed, given the staff survey revealed 40% of employees feel undervalued **[Ap]**. However, democratic leadership can be time-consuming **[An]**, which may be problematic as SwiftLink needs to respond to increased competition in the logistics industry **[Ap]**

An autocratic style would enable Alex to make rapid decisions about opening the new northern depot or flattening the organisational structure **[Ap]**. This could help SwiftLink quickly increase annual revenue from \$15 million to \$20 million **[Ap]** and respond to technologically advanced competitors **[An]**. However, autocratic leadership might further damage employee motivation, potentially worsening the current 29% labour turnover **[Ap]** rate **[An]**

A democratic style would be most appropriate for SwiftLink in its current situation **[E]**. The company is facing significant motivation issues **[Ap] **and needs innovative ideas to tackle challenges like rising fuel costs and increased competition **[Ap]**. Democratic leadership could help address these problems while allowing Alex to make final decisions **[E]**. It would also support the profit-sharing scheme **[Ap] **by giving employees a voice in the company's direction. However, Alex might adopt a more autocratic approach for time-sensitive decisions, such as responding to immediate market threats or finalising the new depot **[Ap]** plans **[E]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Structure**
> 
> - Write one PEA paragraph for each point identified in the question:
> 
>   - Point: Identify the problem
>   - Evidence (Ap): Apply case study detail
>   - Analysis (An): Explain business impact
> - Add a final Evaluation (E):
> 
>   - Decide which problem is easiest/hardest to overcome
>   - Justify your choice
>   - Compare and reject alternatives
> 
> **Marking approach**
> 
> - This is a levelled response answer in which the examiner determines how well you have demonstrated skills of application, analysis and evaluation
> 
>   - Application (4) – Use case study facts
>   - Analysis (4) – Chain effects clearly, using business terms
>   - Evaluation (4) – Balanced judgement, rejects others with reasoning
> 
> **Mark scheme**
> 
> - **Democratic leadership style**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Involves employees in change planning → addresses 40 % feeling undervalued → boosts morale and buy-in
>     - Taps frontline insights on depot operations → improves decision quality and smooths implementation
>     - Builds trust and reduces resistance → essential in a hierarchical structure with low staff engagement
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Decision-making is slower → may delay urgent expansion moves to hit the \$20 m revenue target
>     - Requires extra time and facilitation skills → adds short-term management overhead
> - **Autocratic leadership style**
> 
>   - **Advantages**
>   
>     - Enables rapid decisions on new depot investment, staffing and vehicles → keeps project on schedule
>     - Clear directives reduce ambiguity → useful in a large organisation with five management levels
>   - **Disadvantages**
>   
>     - Risks deepening “undervalued and overworked” sentiment → could worsen 29 % labour turnover in 2022
>     - Stifles employee input → misses valuable operational feedback and may trigger resistance
> - **Conclusion**
> 
>   - Democratic leadership is most appropriate for SwiftLink right now: it tackles poor morale and high turnover by valuing staff input, which in turn supports smoother change adoption
>   - While autocratic can speed up decisions, the cost to motivation and retention—critical issues given a 29 % turnover and 40 % staff dissatisfaction—outweighs its benefits
>   - Alex should combine democratic decision workshops with clear timelines to keep the expansion on track without undermining employee engagement

**Lavelle Manoir Cleaning Products Ltd**

Lavelle Manoir Cleaning Products Ltd is a private limited company that manufactures and sells household cleaning products in Country X. The company was founded 25 years ago and has grown steadily, now employing 150 workers across two production facilities and a head office.

Lavelle Manoir's main products include all-purpose cleaners, laundry detergents, and dishwashing liquids. The company uses flow production methods, with automated production lines for each product category. Lavelle Manoir sources its raw materials from chemical suppliers in Country X and neighbouring countries.

The company has traditionally sold its products through supermarkets and independent retailers in Country X. However, changing consumer preferences for eco-friendly products and increased competition from multinational brands have led to a 15% decline in sales over the past two years. Profits have fallen from \$2.5 million to \$1.8 million during this period.

To address these challenges, Lavelle Manoir's board of directors is considering a significant strategic change. They are debating whether to invest in developing a new line of environmentally friendly cleaning products, or to expand internationally by exporting to the neighbouring Country Y.

The Managing Director, Sarah Chen, believes that developing eco-friendly products could help Lavelle Manoir attract environmentally conscious consumers and improve its brand image. However, the Production Director, John Smith, argues that international expansion would better utilise the company's existing manufacturing capacity and create new market opportunities.

Lavelle Manoir's workforce includes both skilled technicians and production line workers, with many employees having worked for the company for over a decade. The company has a relatively flat organisational structure, with just three levels of hierarchy. However, communication between departments has been identified as an area for improvement.

Recent changes in Country X's economy are also affecting Lavelle Manoir's decision-making. Interest rates have risen by 2%, and there are concerns about a potential economic downturn. Additionally, the government has introduced new regulations on chemical usage and disposal that may increase production costs for cleaning product manufacturers.

Delayering by removing management levels would shorten the chain of command. This could speed up communication between Lavelle Manoir's head office and the two production facilities **[Ap]**. However, with 150 employees, completely flat structures may be impractical, with workers having too little supervision **[An]**

The most effective change would be more formal communication channels **[E]** because it directly addresses Lavelle Manoir's communication issues without drastically altering the existing structure **[E]**. Regular meetings between department heads like Sarah Chen and John Smith **[Ap] **could improve coordination on key decisions **[E]**, such as whether to expand internationally **[Ap]**. Matrix structures or delayering could disrupt Lavelle Manoir's production and impact efficiency during a time of declining sales **[Ap]**. Improving formal communication channels can be gradual, allowing the company to improve coordination between departments while maintaining output **[E]**

>     - The manager expects to be in charge and have all orders followed
>     - Manager keeps themselves separate from the employees
>     - Manager makes all the decisions and keeps information to themselves
>     - Communication is one-way/employees having no opportunity to comment or take part in any decisions about business
>     - Decision-making is quick
>   - Democratic
>

>     - Communication is both downward and upward allowing the experience of employees to be considered by the owners – leading to possibly better decisions being made
>     - Motivating for employees as they feel more involved in the business – less likely to leave/reduced labour turnover
>   - Laissez-faire
>   
>     - Main objectives of the new business are shared with employees but then they are left to organise their own work and take  ecisions without any interference
>     - Communication can be difficult as the leader has little involvement in the decisions being made

>     - Employees can be creative with fresh ideas about how to operate the business
